newsitem.title: USA: Tough disciplinarian tapped as L.A.'s new top cop.
newsitem.headline: Tough disciplinarian tapped as L.A.'s new top cop.

text.p: Los Angeles' highest-ranking black officer was named police chief on Wednesday to combat a racist and undisciplined image plaguing the force since the videotaped beating of Rodney King.

Choosing no-nonsense, 32-year veteran Bernard Parks to head the Los Angeles Police Department, Mayor Richard Riordan also issued a challenge to criminals to expect a crackdown in America's second-largest city.
"Today we put gang members and other criminals on notice, that Los Angeles is not the place for you," the mayor said.

"We will no longer tolerate your tactics of intimidation. We will use every tool in our power to strike you. Simply put: We will fight crime and we will win," Riordan told a City Hall news conference.
"Chief Parks and I pledge to make Los Angeles the safest big city in America."
The mayor earlier denied that race played any role in his choice of Deputy Chief Parks.
"I am angry to think that people would think of Bernie Parks as a black chief," Riordan told the Los Angeles Daily News. "He is the chief of the LAPD, not the black half of the LAPD."
Parks' appointment must be approved by the city council next Tuesday, but sources said it was considered a certainty he would take over the force with its 9,400 officers.

Parks replaces Willie Williams, whose five-year contract was not renewed earlier this year. Williams, who was the city's first black police chief, had been brought in to heal the wounds the LAPD suffered following the 1991 videotaped beating of black motorist King by white officers.

But Williams, who came from Philadelphia, never gained the confidence of officers on the street and Parks was viewed as the insider the force needed to improve its image after the beating of King and the 1992 riots sparked by the acquittal of four officers in the incident.
Asked by Reuters how he would improve morale and help the LAPD move beyond the King beating and the riots in which 53 people died, Parks said: "I don't dwell on the past."
"The department has made tremendous advances, we can't stand still," he said.
He said the top priority for his reforms would be discipline and more involvement with the community.
